lesson.tip: If a scenario mentions a private well, check whether it's been tested — an untested well is the giveaway that something is wrong, even when the water 'looks fine.'

lesson.h: Lighting Intensity: The 50-20-10 Rule That Tracks Risk
lesson.t: Light isn't just for comfort — it's a food-safety control. Employees need enough light to see what they're cutting (for the food and for their own fingers around a blade), to actually read a date label, and to spot spoilage or contamination before it becomes a problem. The Food Code sets minimum light levels, measured in foot-candles, and the number required tracks directly with how risky the task in that area is.
lesson.example:
THE DIM WALK-IN: A walk-in cooler runs on a single weak bulb putting out maybe 5 to 6 foot-candles — well under the 10 foot-candle minimum. A prep cook grabs what she thinks is a fresh tub of diced tomatoes, but in the dim light she can't actually read the date label, which shows the tomatoes are two days past use-by. The food goes into service anyway. Adequate lighting is literally what makes a date label legible enough to catch in the first place.

THE UNDERLIT SLICER STATION: A prep table where a cook runs a meat slicer is lit at only 30 foot-candles, well under the 50 foot-candle minimum required anywhere knives, slicers, or grinders are in use. That number exists as much for the cook's fingers as for the food.
bullets: 50 foot-candles minimum: surfaces where employees use knives, slicers, grinders, or saws (food safety AND employee safety)
20 foot-candles minimum: handwashing sinks, warewashing areas, and self-service areas like buffets and salad bars
10 foot-candles minimum: walk-in refrigeration units, dry storage areas, and general dining areas
Light fixtures over food-prep, food-storage, and food-display areas must be shielded or shatter-resistant so a broken bulb can't drop glass into food
The tiers exist for both food-safety reasons (reading labels, spotting spoilage) and employee-safety reasons (working safely around blades)
lesson.why: The foot-candle tiers track the risk of the task in that spot: cutting with a blade demands the sharpest vision (50 fc), reading labels and washing hands correctly needs solid general visibility (20 fc), and just navigating a storage room or dining area safely needs the least (10 fc). Shielding matters for a separate reason — an unshielded bulb that shatters over an open prep surface turns a light fixture into a physical contamination hazard in an instant.
lesson.memory: 🧠 LIGHTING: 50 fc = Knives/Slicers/Prep. 20 fc = Handwash/Warewash/Self-Service. 10 fc = Walk-in/Dry Storage/Dining. All fixtures over food = shielded or shatter-resistant.
lesson.tip: Learn the pattern 50-20-10 tied to task risk, not just the raw numbers in isolation. The exam will describe an activity or a location and ask for the minimum foot-candles — identify the AREA TYPE first, then apply the right number.

lesson.h: Ventilation and Hood Systems: Where the Byproduct of Cooking Has to Go
lesson.t: Cooking produces a lot more than food — heat, steam, smoke, grease-laden vapor, odors. All of it needs somewhere to go besides settling right back down onto food, equipment, and surfaces. Ventilation systems, especially the exhaust hoods over your cooking equipment, exist to capture and remove that byproduct before it turns into a contamination problem, a fire problem, or both.
lesson.example:
THE UNCLEANED HOOD FILTERS: A restaurant's exhaust hood filters haven't been cleaned in months. Grease has built up so thick the hood can barely pull vapor upward anymore, so most of it drifts sideways across the cook line instead, leaving a thin greasy film on nearby prep surfaces and utensils. Beyond the contamination, the grease caked inside the hood and ductwork is now a serious fire hazard — a grease fire that starts inside an exhaust system spreads fast, because the whole hood is basically a chimney full of fuel at that point.

THE CONDENSATION DRIP: A walk-in cooler's evaporator unit doesn't have a working condensate drain pan, so water drips straight from the ceiling onto open cases of ready-to-eat deli meat stored below. It's not a hood-and-cook-line scenario, but the principle is identical: uncontrolled moisture from mechanical systems can never be allowed to touch food.
bullets: Exhaust hoods over cooking equipment remove grease-laden vapor, heat, steam, and smoke before it settles on food and surfaces
Ventilation overall must control excess heat, humidity, and condensation throughout the whole kitchen, not just at the cook line
Grease filters must be cleaned and maintained on a regular schedule — buildup is both a contamination hazard and a fire hazard
Exhaust air should vent to the outside, not recirculate cooking byproduct back into prep or dining areas
Condensation from any overhead source — pipes, refrigeration units, ductwork — must never be allowed to drip onto food or food-contact surfaces
lesson.why: Grease-laden vapor that never gets captured doesn't just disappear — it settles as a sticky film on every nearby surface, and over time it accumulates inside the hood system itself into a genuine fire risk. Proper ventilation removes both problems at once: the contamination hazard and the fire hazard that grows alongside it.
lesson.memory: 🧠 VENTILATION = Remove grease, heat, steam, smoke, condensation, odors — vented OUTSIDE, never recirculated. Dirty hood filters = fire hazard, not just a cleaning issue.
lesson.tip: If a scenario mentions grease film on surfaces, smoke lingering in the kitchen, or condensation dripping onto food, think ventilation system failure. The fix is proper hood and exhaust maintenance — not just wiping down whatever surface got hit.

lesson.h: The Building Itself Is Equipment: Floors, Walls, Garbage, and Pest-Proofing
lesson.t: Floors, walls, and ceilings in food-prep and storage areas need the exact same core standard as your equipment: smooth, durable, easily cleanable — just scaled up to the size of the whole room. And beyond the surfaces themselves, how you contain garbage, where restrooms sit, and how well the building actually keeps pests out all decide whether your kitchen stays clean day to day or slowly loses that fight.
lesson.example:
COVING AT THE FLOOR-WALL JOINT: An older kitchen has a standard sharp 90-degree corner where the floor meets the wall. Grease, moisture, and food debris collect there because no mop or cloth can actually get into a tight right angle — it becomes a permanent buildup zone no matter how often the floor gets mopped. A renovated kitchen next door has coving instead: a rounded, sealed transition between floor and wall. The same corner wipes clean in one pass, because there's no sharp angle left for anything to hide in.

THE OVERFLOWING DUMPSTER: A restaurant's outdoor garbage containers are missing their lids and sit right against the back door, overflowing after a busy weekend. The open, uncovered trash pulls in flies and rodents, and because the containers sit right at the entrance, anything drawn to the garbage has a short trip straight into the building. Covered, well-maintained containers on a proper pad, positioned away from the doors, remove both the attraction and the easy access point at once.
bullets: Floors, walls, and ceilings in food areas must be smooth, durable, and easily cleanable
Coving — a curved, sealed floor-to-wall transition — eliminates the hard-to-clean 90-degree corner where grime and moisture collect
Garbage and refuse containers must be durable, leak-proof, and covered, and emptied often enough that they never overflow
Restrooms must be conveniently located and equipped with a self-closing door and a handwashing sink
Gaps, cracks, and unsealed openings around pipes, walls, and doors should be sealed — every opening is a potential pest entry point
Good facility design isn't decoration — it's a pest-exclusion and cleanability system built directly into the structure
lesson.why: Pests and bacteria exploit the exact same weaknesses: places that are hard to see, hard to reach, and hard to clean. A sharp uncoved corner, an unsealed pipe penetration, an uncovered trash can — each one is a small design gap that, multiplied across an entire building, becomes a dependable pathway for contamination or infestation. Designing the space to eliminate those gaps up front beats trying to clean or exterminate your way out of a design flaw after the fact.
lesson.memory: 🧠 FACILITY DESIGN = Smooth/durable/cleanable surfaces + Coving at floor-wall joints + Covered leak-proof garbage + Restrooms with self-closing doors and a sink + No unsealed gaps for pests.
lesson.tip: Coving questions test whether you understand WHY it matters, not just that it exists — the answer is always about eliminating a hard-to-clean corner where debris builds up. Garbage and pest-exclusion questions usually describe one specific gap or failure (a missing lid, an unsealed pipe) and ask you to name the risk it creates.
